However, two contrast- ing interpretations of the Gondwana apparent polar wander (APW) path have yet to be resolved [Van der Voo, 1988; Briden, 1992]. Because paleomagnetic data from Australia [Hurley and Van der Voo, 1987] and Africa [Hargraves et al., 1987] dominate the discussion, we attempted to determine Paleozoic paleomagnetic poles for Gondwana through paleo- magnetic study of South America. Samples were taken from Paleozoic red sedimentary strata across the Eastern Cordillera and sub-Andean Belt of Bolivia. Acquisition of a large paleo- magnetic data set from this region, however, forced us to the conclusion that the sampled strata have been affected by widespread chemical remagnetization probably during or just preceding Cenozoic folding. The results of this study are of significance to paleomag- netic analyses undertaken elsewhere. We report here well- determined site-mean characteristic directions of natural rema- nent magnetism (NRM) from some Paleozoic red sedimentary rocks which have been interpreted previously to possess a primary magnetization [Ernesto et al., 1988]. Samples were oriented using both magnetic compass and solar compass. No significant deviations were noted between these orientation methods. An additional 14 samples were taken from slumped blocks at one particular level of the Vilavila Formation. The preservation of recognizable bedding in these slump blocks allowed us to use these samples in a modified conglomerate test. Following sample preparation, all specimens were stored and analyzed in a magnetically shielded room with background field intensity < 200 nT. NRM was measured with a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer (2G model 755R). Thermal demagne- tizations at 14 to 18 steps up to 680øC were accomplished using furnaces with magnetic field intensity less than 10 nT in the sample region. Results of thermal demagnetization were analyzed by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and site-mean directions were determined using the statistical methods of Fisher [1953]. Analyses of coercivity spectra of 11 representative samples were performed using the methods of Dunlop [1972] and Lowrie [1990]. Factors limiting the precision with which the characteristic directions can be used to infer age of remagnetization and tec- tonic disturbance subsequent to remagnetization include the following: (1) The major variation in bedding attitudes within the Pongo sampling area allows the percent of folding at remagnetization to be fairly tightly constrained to 20% fold- ing (Figure 7). However, the major sampled stratigraphic sequence at Villamontes is nearly homoclinal and that section has only a modest contrast of bedding attitude with other sam- pling localities in that region. Accordingly, assignment of percent folding at the time of remagnetization of Paleozoic strata at Villamontes lacks precision (Figure 8). (2) The mag- nitude of APW as viewed from South America is modest during Mesozoic and Cenozoic time [Irving and Irving, 1982; Besse and Courtillot, 1991]. Future attempts to obtain primary paleomagnetic directions from Paleozoic rocks of the Andes should focus on less deformed regions, per- haps in the forebulge region of the active foreland basin. Finally, the documentation of this remagnetization reaffirms the critical importance of multiple field tests of paleomagnetic stability when applying paleomagnetic methods to rocks in orogenic zones. An additional 14 samples were taken from slumped blocks at one particular level of the Vilavila Formation. The preservation of recognizable bedding in these slump blocks allowed us to use these samples in a modified conglomerate test. Following sample preparation, all specimens were stored and analyzed in a magnetically shielded room with background field intensity < 200 nT. NRM was measured with a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer (2G model 755R). Discussion and Conclusions One ancient direction of magnetization (component B) has been clearly identified in these Lower Devonian sediments from north- ern France. Unfortunately, it was not possible to carry out a meaningful fold test on the results owing to the relatively uniform structural attitude of the sediments. However, the sample and site mean directions (11 sites) are extremely well grouped (Figure 8) and are not similar to any younger directions of magnetization expected for this locality. Thus component B is considered to be primary in origin, and closely linked with the rock age. After removal of a present-day overprint, a higher unblocking temperature component of magnetization is identified (the B direction) which yields an overall mean direction of 222ø/+35 ø, k= 121.6, a 95=4.2ø after bedding correction, 11 sites. No fold test is possible, but the presence of a thin sill allowed sampling for a contact test, the results of which are positive. Thus the B direction of magnetization is considered to be primary in origin and closely bracketed with the rock age. The resulting paleopole (315øE, 13øS) corresponds to a paleolatitude of 19øS for the Armorican Massif, placing it adjacent to the southern margin of Baltica and Avalonia. This clearly demonstrates for the first time that this sector of the Rheic Ocean had closed by Early Devonian times, and that the Armorican Massif was in its present-day orientation with respect to Baltica. These data, however, are rather poorly defined, and the paleogeographic setting for this part of Armorica, as well as the timing of suturing with Avalonia, remains unclear. For Carboniferous times, paleomagnetic data demonstrate that there were significant amounts of internal rotation, oroclinal bending, and deformation within the Variscan fold belt [Bachtadse and Van der Voo, 1986; Perroud, 1986; Tait et al., 1996; Van der Voo et al., 1997]. This deformation clearly postdates the rotation within the Bohemian Massif which occurred prior to the Famennian, and is most likely related to late stage compression of the orogen and the collision of Gondwana to the south. In summary, the dynamics involved and interaction of the various units consituting Armorica in Siluro-Devonian times and timing of closure of the more easterly segment of the Rheic Ocean between the Armorican Massif and eastern Avalonia remain un- certain. K-Ar age dates show that the welded tuffs erupted between 66 Ma and 46 Ma. All sites yield reliable paleomagnetic directions, with unblocking temperatures higher than 560°C. The high-temperature component at 12 sites and the medium-temperature component at 3 sites in the Bogopol Group show reversed polarity (D = 193.7”, Z = - 57.6”, ff 95 = 8.10). The high-temperature component at 11 sites in the Sijanov Group showed both reversed and normal polarities and its mean direction reveals no detectable deflection from north (D = - 2.9”, Z = 59.6”, a95 = 11.2”). The combined paleomagnetic direction of the two groups yields a paleomagnetic pole of 250.5”E, 84.1”N (A,, = 8.8”), which falls near Cretaceous paleomagnetic poles from Outer Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, the North China Block and the Sout

ral strike-slip faults. Movements on these faults were either contemporaneous with, or slightly earlier than, the Late Cretaceous vol- canic activity [9]. Recent geological and geophysical studies sug- gest that the opening of back arc basins along the Eurasian continental margin has been in progress since the India-Asian collision occurred at about 45 Ma: the Japan Sea, the Okinawa Trough and the South China Sea were created later than 32 Ma [4-71. The opening of the South China Sea was accompanied by large, continental, tectonic rotation of the Indochina block and left-lateral strike-slip motion along the Red River fault sys- tem 161. Hence, the opening process of back arc basins seems to be associated with deformation of the continental margin as a consequence of the ongoing impingement of the Indian subcontinent into Asia. Formation of the Japan Sea-Japan arc system is one of the major tectonic events along the Eurasian continental coast. The Sikhote Alin mountain area is located in the easternmost part of the Eurasian continental margin, bordering the northern Japan Sea (Fig. 1A). This study focuses on the Sikhote Alin area and uses paleomag- rietism to investigate continental deformation as- sociated with the Japan Sea opening. In this paper we pres

Mid-Cretaceous volcanic rocks con- sist of andesitic feldspar porphyry flows and tuffs of the Mount Nansen Group. Felsic volcanic rocks deposited across south- central Yukon between 84 and 78 Ma, including pyroclastic flows and flow-banded rhyolite, are included in the Windy–Table Suite (Mihalynuk et al. 1992; Hart 1995). Vo- luminous sequences of subaerial volcanic rocks deposited across central Yukon between 72 and 69 Ma, including exten- sive flood basalts, are included in the Carmacks Group (Tem- pelman-Kluit 1974; Grond et al. 1984). Paleomagnetic field and laboratory procedures Drill cores (typically six) or hand samples (three) were col- lected at each site and oriented using both magnetic and solar compasses. The solar and magnetic bearings agreed within 2° except where the rocks had been hit by lightning and were, as a consequence, strongly magnetic. Solar bearings were used for these rocks. Specimens were measured in the laboratory using a robotized Schonstedt DSM1 fluxgate magnetometer or a Geofyzika JR5A spinner magnetometer. Specimens were de- magnetized using five to 10 demagnetization steps, using a Schonstedt TSD-1 therm

Three sites (W61–W63) were collected from isolated outcrops along the Klondike Highway north of Carmacks. It appears, therefore, that, like the Mandanna Member, the Nordenskiöld Formation at this locality was totally overprinted, after tilting, at the time of extrusion of the Carmacks Group. The interpretation for the Cinnamon Bun Row locality re- manence is less straightforward. The mean direction before tectonic correction is nearly vertical, which implies magneti- zation at the north pole. But after tectonic correction, the di- rection is shallow even compared with the Carmacks remanence. There are at least three ways this result can be interpreted: (i) the remanence could be primary, but it is shal- low compared with other Jurassic paleomagnetic data obtained in the southern Intermontane Belt (e.g., Monger and Irving 1980); (ii) the remanence could be a predeformational Creta- ceous overprint, implying an approximately 60° clockwise vertical axis rotation; and (iii) the remanence could be a post- deformational Cretaceous overprint followed by a further tilt of 20° down towards 347°NNW. Tilts of this magnitude have been observed in the Carmacks Formation elsewhere and so it is not unreasonable to invoke a late tilt. This explains the dis- crepancy between the locality mean direction of Cinnamon Bun Row (tilted after being overprinted during extrusion of the Carmacks Group) and that of Atlin Lake (not tilted after over- printing), and we favour this interpretation. Conclusions The results of this paleomagnetic study of fluorspar ores and their host rocks in the Illinois-Kentucky dis- trict lead to the following conclusions: 1. Mississippian limestones from some 200 km to the northeast near Louisville, which are stratigraphi- cally equivalent to the host rocks, retain an A charac- teristic RM component. From stratigraphic data Kolata and Nelson (1991) estimate uplift at between 2.4 and 4.6 km. Similarly, Leach et al. This uplift must be assumed to have been in response to large intra- plate tectonic forces and to have caused a major pe- riod of reactivation on the fluorspar district faults. Conclusions The results of this paleomagnetic study of fluorspar ores and their host rocks in the Illinois-Kentucky dis- trict lead to the following conclusions: 1. Mississippian limestones from some 200 km to the northeast near Louisville, which are stratigraphi- cally equivalent to the host rocks, retain an A charac- teristic RM component. It resides in single domain to pseudosingle domain magnetite and has a reversed polarization. A gives a mid-Pennsylvanian pole posi- tion that is typical of Kiaman remagnetization of older Paleozoic limestones throughout much of the U. S. midcontinent. 2. These results show that the hydrothermal dolomite sheets and associated Mississippi Valley-type deposits were formed with a primary chemical characteristic remanent mag- netization during Late Cretaceous Laramide uplift and defor- mation. It follows, therefore, that Laramide structures will provide one control for Mississippi Valley-type mineralization in the southern Rocky Mountains. The results also show that the Cambrian dolostone host rocks were either limestones which were dolomitized to acquire a primary remanence or dolostones which were recrystallized to acquire a reset sec- ondary remanence during the Late Cretaceous. Beview of the evidence to date leads to the conclusion that the most significant fluid flow event in the western Canada sedimentary basin occurred in response to the Lara- mide orogeny. The stratigraphic, structural, palcomagnetic, fission track, hydrogeologic modeling, and most other cited evidence supports this statement. Also, the available fluid inclusion, geochemical, and isotopic evidence can be ratio- nally explained in terms of an evolving fluid in the western Canada sedimentary basin from the peak of the Laramide orogeny to the present. Experimental Methods Sampling A total of 405 oriented core specimens were prepared from 106 block samples from 32 sites (Figs. i and 2). Oliver (1986, 1992) noted the relationship on a continental scale between orogenesis and the spots and stains of the related fluid flows that include regional dolomitization, transport of petroleum into reservoirs, and the formation of Mississippi Valley-type zinc-lead-barite deposits. It intrudes granulite-rank Archean gneisses in the Kapuskasing Structural Zone of the Wawa Subprovince in the Superior Province of the Canadian Shield. It adjoins the Ivanhoe Lake fault zone, which forms the boundary with the Abitibi Subprovince and is the probable locus of maximum motion between the subprovinces. Specimens from 18 sites in the complex were analyzed paleomagnetically by alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and by saturation isothermal remanence tests. Large, recent viscous remanence components required removal before a stable remanence with a mean direction of 305.4", 64.1" (a,, = 5.2") was isolated. Its pole of 53.7"N, 156.5"W (dp = 6.7", dm = 8.3") indicates emplacement at 1108 f 10 Ma during a brief normal interval in a predominantly reversed-polarity time. This study indicates that there has been no postintrusion tilting of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone and that postintrusion uplift by unroofing did not exceed about 8 km. They have been cut by the Early Proterozoic Hearst diabase dikes, which trend north-south and dip nearly vertically (Emst and Halls 1984). The complex is nearly circular, with a diameter of about 5.5 km. It comprises dominantly massive, coarse-grained leucocratic nepheline syenite that forms both the core and the periphery. In between are arcuate bands and partial rings of foliated malignite - ijolite that dip at 40° - 65 towards the centre. Within these bands on the north side is a small zone of calcic carbonatite. On the west side of these bands is an inte- rior zone of iiolite breccia, with abundant magnetite, and on the north side is an exterior zone of ijolite breccia called the Portage Lake Complex. The syenite and mafic alkalic rocks are cut in turn by carbonatite veins with pyrochlore that carry the niobium values, by the apatite - magnetite veins, and finally by occasional lamprophyre dikes that are not exposed. The contacts of the complex are apparently vertical, and the adjacent wall rocks are fenitized. There is no petrologic evi- dence of postintrusive metamorphism of the complex. It intrudes granulite-rank Archean gneisses in the Kapuskasing Structural Zone of the Wawa Subprovince in the Superior Province of the Canadian Shield. Specimens from 18 sites in the complex were analyzed paleomagnetically by alternating-field and thermal demagnetization and by saturation isothermal remanence tests. Its pole of 53.7"N, 156.5"W (dp = 6.7", dm = 8.3") indicates emplacement at 1108 f 10 Ma during a brief normal interval in a predominantly reversed-polarity time. Laboratory Methods At least two cylindrical specimens were cut from each core or drilled from each block sample. Usually, one specimen from each sample was subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization up to 100 mT using a Schonstedt GSD-1 instrument, and the remanent magnetiz- ation was measured on a modified DIGICO spinner magneto- meter. About one third of duplicate specimens were sub- jected to thermal demagnetization in at least 11 steps up to 625øC using a Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer. Components of magnetization were analyzed using orthogonal vector plots [Zijderveld, 1967], and their direc- tions were determined using principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980] with a maximum angular deviation of <10 ø (mostly <5 ø) and number of data points > 3. Magnetiz- ation directions of specimens from the same sample that disagreed by more than 30 ø were rejected; otherwise, data were combined to give sample mean directions. Finally, dike/site mean and overall mean directions were calculated using Fisher's [1953] statistics. Analyses of Magnetiz

lose to that of the present Earth's field (PEF: D=5.8ø/I=79.9ø; e.g., Figures 2c, 2d, 2g, 2k, and 21), suggesting that it is a recent viscous remanent magnetization (VRM). After removal of the VRM, a stable remanence is defined, giving linear trajectories of magnetization towards the origin of the orthogonal plots. Based on differences of magnetization directions, the stable remanence comprises three components: A (south declination with a steep downward inclination), B (WSW declination with a steep downward inclination), and C (ENE-ESE declination with a steep upward inclination). All three components have an intermediate to high-coercivity range (20-100 mT). Their thermal decay curves are all square-shouldered with unblocking temperatures typically between 550 and 580øC. These features suggest that relative- ly pure single/pseudo-single domain magnetite is the domi- nant remanence carrier. Duplicate specimens respond to AF and thermal demagnetizations in similar ways (e.g., Figures 2a/2b, 2e/2f, and 2i/2j), indicating that all three components are reliable. The majority of dikes in the Pikwitonei Domain give excellent results on demagnetization. However, at Molson Lake and particularly at Cross Lake, rocks with unstable or erratic magnetizations are pervasive (s

ted to magnetite produced from varying degrees of deuteric hydrothermal alteration of olivine or orthopyroxene [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975]. The reason why remanent magnetizations in the Molson dikes are best preserved in the Pikwitonei Domain is probably due to the relatively dry state of the host rocks. As a consequence, deuteric alteration of the dikes is either reduced or absent. Host granulites always carry the same stable component as that of their adjacent dikes up to about 1-2 dike widths away from their contacts (Figures 3a-3f). Thermal decay curves of host rocks near contacts show square-shouldered patterns with narrow unblocking temperatures close to the Curie point of magnetite (Figures 3b, 3d, and 3f). These results suggest that both dikes and baked host rocks acquired their remanence at similar temperatures and times. Farther away, however, a consistent predike magnetization compo- nent D is observed regardless of what remanence is carried by the dike (Figures 3g-3i). The frequency of dike intrusion increases toward and within the belt. Molson dikes range from ultramafic to mafic in composi- tion. Chemically, they display characteristics of tholeiitic basalts [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975] and komatiites [Scoates and Macek, 1978] which have rift-type chemical affinities [Baragar and Scoates, 1981; Scoates, 1981]. Olivine, orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, plagioclase, and hornblende represent initial crystallization phases. Opaque minerals are mainly chromite, magnetite with ilmenite lamellae, and minor fine-grained sulphide minerals occurring as inclusions in hornblende, such as pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite, and pyrite [Scoates and Macek, 1978]. Within the Thompson Belt the Molson dikes were deformed and metamorphosed during the Trans-Hudson Orogen. The dikes southeast of the belt, however, generally escaped this event. In the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province, deuteric alteration of olivine to magnetite and serpentine occurs and varying degrees of crystal fractionation features are developed [Ermanovics and Fahrig, 1975]. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. investigate the paleomagnetism of the Molson dikes as a function of distance from the CSBZ. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. investigate the paleomagnetism of the Molson dikes as a function of distance from the CSBZ. An initial reconnaissance survey [Halls et al., 1990] showed that westward within the Thompson Belt they became magneti- cally more unstable as the degree of metamorphism associ- ated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen increased. Here we emphasize results from dikes within the Superior Province to the east and particularly within the Pikwitonei Domain where previous paleomagnetic experience, with granulites of the Kapuskasing zone [Costanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons and Vandall, 1990], suggests that host rock stability may allow definitive baked contact tests. Our principal objectives are to document differences in remanent magnetiz- ation within the Molson swarm that might define a multi- intrusive history and to interpret these data in terms of tectonic setting and their significance in the development of the Trans-Hudson Orogen. Geology Molson Dike Swarm The swarm intrudes the lower-grade terrain of the Superior Province and the Pikwitonei Domain. Dikes found in the Thompson Belt and in the Split Lake Block are believed to be equivalent to the Molson dikes on the basis of chemical 21,717 21,718 ZHAI ET AL.' Field and Laboratory Methods Field Methods Sampling areas were located at Cross and Molson Lakes in the lower-grade Superior Province, at Sipiwesk, Landing, Cauchon, Pikwitonei, and Witchai Lakes in the Pikwitonei Domain, and at Paint Lake in the Thompson Belt (Figure 1). A total of 92 sites representing about 75 dikes were sampled. Samples were obtained at variable distances from dike margins wherever possible, with a majority taken from fine-grained parts or chilled margins. When available, host granulites adjacent to and remote from dikes were also collected for baked contact tests. In addition, fine-grained granulites, at least 1 km from any known dike, were sampled throughout Landing and Pikwitonei Lakes (sites CR1 and CR2, see Table 1) in an attempt to retrieve a pre-Molson dike remanence. Further sites were sampled from fine- grained and reworked granulites at Paint Lake to examine the influence of the Trans-Hudson Orogen on the paleomag- netism. Samples were mostly field drilled at Molson, Landing, Pikwitonei, Paint, Cauchon, and Witchai Lakes and block sampled elsewhere. Sun and magnetic compasses were used for each sample orientation. Both types of arguments are reexamined here. Using a new model of the Atlantic Ocean evolution described elsewhere, it is shown that the reconstructions of the positions of Africa relative to North America before the Atlantic opening, and at the times of magnetic anomalies M22 and J, do not imply a major motion of Morocco independent of Africa during these periods of time. The corresponding geomagnetic paleopoles have been recomputed from sample sites located on both "mobile" Morocco and "stable" Africa. The results indicate that the virtual geomagnetic pole of "mobile" Morocco for the Liassic falls within the 95% confidence cone of "stable" Africa. It is thus concluded that no major movement has occurred between "mobile" Morocco and "stable" Africa during the early phases of opening of the central Atlantic Ocean. target_context.excerpt: kaline rocks Regional geology The late Cretaceous alkaline ~trusions of the Eastern Desert may be divided for convenience into three groups. The first, the trachytic (boston- itic) dikes, sills and plugs (B sites) intrude into the sediments of the Ham- mamet Formation and surrounding metamorphic rocks of the basement complex in the region southwest of Quseir (Fig. 1). Several of these units have been affected by uranium mineralization and these have been studied in detail by Hussein and El Kassas (1971, 1972). In the field the rocks usually form prominent relief and are recognizable by their light colored fine-grained character. 171 The rocks are composed predominantly of alkali feldspar and subordinate

he mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N

m in the eastern desert of Egypt: paieomagnetic, chemical and K-Ar evi- dence. In: J.H. Illies (Editor), Mechanism of Graben Formation. Tectonophysics, 73: 169-193. Paleomagnetic and radiometric data confirm the existence of two phases of igneous activity in the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic history of eastern Egypt. In the mid to late Cretaceous, the earlier and more extensive episode produced the Wadi Natash alkaline basalts and numerous small traehytic intrusions. The ring complexes of Abu Khrug and Gebel El Kahfa were also emplaced at this time. The mean paleopole position for the intrusive rocks is at 65.3’N 111.2OW, Agg = 11.4 (31 sites). Chemical analyses of the trachytes show that they are enriched in Nb, Zr and Y and depleted in Sr, Ba, Cr and Ni suggesting either prolonged fractionation or limited partial fusion. The second phase of activity, during Oligo-Miocene time, is represented by small tholeiitic basalt flows on the Red Sea coast and along the Nile valley. The mean paleopole position for the flows is at 68.2”N 101,5”E, A 95 = 27.8 (3 sites). The wide scatter is inter- preted as reflecting secular variation. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of conti

asin col- lapse, and to transport of sediment towards the axial valley. Approximately 50 m.y. after the initial uplift, continental separation accompanied by tholei- itic volcanism begins. This takes no account of the subsequent spreading behaviour, that is, it is independent of the two spreading stages, proposed and discussed by Girdler and Styles (1976), Davidson and Rex (1980) and Richardson and Harrison (1976). PAL~OMAGNETIC AND RA~~OM~TR~C STUDY Alkaline rocks Regional geology The late Cretaceous alkaline ~trusions of the Eastern Desert may be divided for convenience into three groups. The first, the trachytic (boston- itic) dikes, sills and plugs (B sites) intrude into the sediments of the Ham- mamet Formation and surrounding metamorphic rocks of the basement complex in the region southwest of Quseir (Fig. 1). Several of these units have been affected by uranium mineralization and these have been studied in detail by Hussein and El Kassas (1971, 1972). In the field the rocks usually form prominent relief and are recognizable by their light colored fine-grained character. 171 The rocks are composed predominantly of alkali feldspar and subordinate quartz, ferromagnesian minerals, zircon and apatite. In the absence of the radial arrangement of the feldspar la

In the absence of the radial arrangement of the feldspar laths, considered diagnostic of bostonites, it is suggested here that the rocks be called by the more familiar term, trachyte. El Manharawy (1972) quoted Rb-Sr ages for these rocks ranging from 300 m.y. to 74 m.y. despite the gross similarity of the rocks. Recent K-Ar dates of these rocks, however, give a much closer grouping of ages from 63 m.y. to 92 m.y. (Table I). As indicated earlier there are two phases of igneous activity, the first being volumetrically much more extensive than the second. The opening of the earlier phase was marked by the extrusion of alkaline basalts of which the Wadi Natash lavas are the best known (El Shazly and Krs, 1973), although slightly older lavas are reported from the. Wadi Amba in the northern Eastern Desert. The paleopole position of the lavas is indis- tinguishable from those obtained from the intrusions reported here. The radiometric age dates and the meagre fauna from the basal Nubian Sandstone Formation (Ward and McDonald, 1979) are consistent with a late Cretaceous age for the igneous units. The paleopole positions compare closely with those from other African rocks of similar age, on the assumption of zero relative motion between the Nubian and other African plates (Fig. 11). The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of continental rifting to the northern Red Sea. The earlier, alkaline phase of igneous activity is related to regional up- lift while the second, tholeiitic phase is associated with widening of the rift valley. I. With relatively few radiometric dates available, most workers have had to rely upon field criteria and composition to attempt a classification of the intrusions. Commonly these were grouped, from oldest to youngest, as acidic, intermediate, basic and alkaline intrusions. In the course of three field seasons we have collected samples from some 200 sites in the igneous rocks. The results to date suggest that the majority of these, including most of the acidic, intermediate and basic intrusions, are associated with the closing stages of the Pan-African event (Davies et al., 1980). The remaining, younger rocks include some which were emplaced since the mid to late Cretaceous and which constitute the subject of this paper. Igneous activity since the mid to late Cretaceous occurred in two district phases which we relate to the tectonic history of the northern Red Sea. The chronological and chemical data are used with studies of sedimentary forma- tions coeval with the igneous rocks to apply a general model of continental rifting to the northern Red Sea. With relatively few radiometric dates available, most workers have had to rely upon field criteria and composition to attempt a classification of the intrusions. Commonly these were grouped, from oldest to youngest, as acidic, intermediate, basic and alkaline intrusions. In the course of three field seasons we have collected samples from some 200 sites in the igneous rocks. The results to date suggest that the majority of these, including most of the acidic, intermediate and basic intrusions, are associated with the closing stages of the Pan-African event (Davies et al., 1980). The remaining, younger rocks include some which were emplaced since the mid to late Cretaceous and which constitute the subject of this paper. Igneous activity since the mid to late Cretaceous occurred in two district phases which we relate to the tectonic history of the northern Red Sea. With relatively few radiometric dates available, most workers have had to rely upon field criteria and composition to attempt a classification of the intrusions. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. The Itati- aia massif is structurally linked to the SE Brazilian continental rift, which developed in an ENE to EW trending transcurrent system by the end of the BrasiI- iano (Pan African) Cycle and which was reactivated during the breakup of Gondwana [18]. The alkaline complex is composed of syenites, foyaites, pulask- ites, quartz syenites, magmatic breccias and alkaline granite [19]. The mean K-Ar age obtained on ten biotites from the Itatiaia rocks is 70.5 f 3.3 Ma [10,12]. 2.3. Passa Quatro complex The Passa Quatro alkaline complex (148 km*, Fig. 2) is close to the Itatiaia complex. It was emplaced into the Precambrian metamorphic com- plexes of Juiz de Fora, Paraiba do Sul and the Aqungui Group [7,17]. The main lithological types are alkali plutonic rocks (nepheline syenites) with minor phonolitic dykes. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. The Itati- aia massif is structurally linked to the SE Brazilian continental rift, which developed in an ENE to EW trending transcurrent system by the end of the BrasiI- iano (Pan African) Cycle and which was reactivated during the breakup of Gondwana [18]. The alkaline complex is composed of syenites, foyaites, pulask- ites, quartz syenites, magmatic breccias and alkaline granite [19]. The mean K-Ar age obtained on ten biotites from the Itatiaia rocks is 70.5 f 3.3 Ma [10,12]. 2.3. Passa Quatro complex The Passa Quatro alkaline complex (148 km*, Fig. 2) is close to the Itatiaia complex. It was emplaced into the Precambrian metamorphic com- plexes of Juiz de Fora, Paraiba do Sul and the Aqungui Group [7,17]. The main lithological types are alkali plutonic rocks (nepheline syenites) with minor phonolitic dykes. section_candidates.excerpt: Itatiaia complex The Itatiaia alkaline complex (220 km’, Fig. 2) is located on the boundary between the states of Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais. This intrudes into the Precambrian basement, which is represented by the Juiz de Fora metamorphic complex [7,17]. The Itati- aia massif is structurally linked to the SE Brazilian continental rift, which developed in an ENE to EW trending transcurrent system by the end of the BrasiI- iano (Pan African) Cycle and which was reactivated during the breakup of Gondwana [18]. The alkaline complex is composed of syenites, foyaites, pulask- ites, quartz syenites, magmatic breccias and alkaline granite [19]. The mean K-Ar age obtained on ten biotites from the Itatiaia rocks is 70.5 f 3.3 Ma [10,12]. 2.3. Passa Quatro complex The Passa Quatro alkaline complex (148 km*, Fig. 2) is close to the Itatiaia complex. It was emplaced into the Precambrian metamorphic com- plexes of Juiz de Fora, Paraiba do Sul and the Aqungui Group [7,17]. The main lithological types are alkali plutonic rocks (nepheline syenites) with minor phonolitic dykes. FEDORENKO Central Institute for Mineral Exploration (TsNIGRI), Varshavskoye Shosse 129B, 113545 Moscow, Russia Abstract The volcanic sequence of the Noril'sk area, northern Siberia, provides the most complete section of early Siberian flood-basalt volcanism. Paleomagnetic measurements for more than 4000 samples of lava and tuff indicate that nearly all of this >3500-m-thick sequence was laid down during one interval of normal magnetic polarity. Lavas of the lower third of this sequence are cut by the ore-bearing Noril'sk-I intrusion, which has an age of 251 Ma, identical to that of the Permian-Triassic boundary. Thus, the normal-polarity interval represented by this sequence is inferred to be the first of the Triassic Period. Eruption of this enormous volume of material in a relatively brief period coincident with the earth's greatest mass extinction requires that all aspects of Siberian flood-basalt volcanism be evaluated carefully as possibly contributing to that catastrophe. Stepwise thermal demagnetization of the subaerial mafic volcanics of the Ludlovian Fivemile Brook Formation of northwestern Maine reveals two ancient high-temperature, dual-polarity remanences. Fivemile Brook results AMS results indicate a low degree of anisotropy, indicating minimal probability of remanence deflec- tion. The ratios of bulk susceptibilities at 77 K to those at room temperature (293 K) indicate involve- ment of a paramagnetic mineral phase that is proba- bly chlorite. Moreover, the magnetic fabric observed in a number of Fivemile Brook sites is roughly cleavage parallel. Based on high unblocking temperatures it is in- ferred that both the c- and b-components are carried by hematite. In view of the extremely high tem- peratures required to thermally reset hematite grains (Pullaiah et al., 1976), both the c- and b-components are presumably chemical remanent magnetizations (CRMs) resulting from hematite replacement of orig- inal magnetite. Subaerial weathering may account for initial oxidation of the magnetite in these vol- canics; a later CRM may be associated with fluid circulation (Dorobek, 1989). A tilt-corrected mean direction yields an inclination of 41 ° (~rl = 3.9 °, N = 4 sites) and the magnetization is interpreted as a near-primary magnetization acquired well before the end of Early Devonian deformation. An in situ mean direction (D = 165 °, 1 = 35 °, ~gs = 6 °, k = 65, N = 10 entries from 8 sites), is interpreted as a secondary overprint with a pole (22°S, 306°E) near the Early Carboniferous segment of the North American apparent polar wander path (APWP). The inclination-only fold test peaks at 50% unfolding with a mean inclination of -35 ° (~ = 8.5 °, n = 148). Synfolding acquisition of magnetization is Wenlockian, based on a negative conglomerate test at the base of the section and a positive conglomerate test at the top of the section. Clockwise streaking of site mean directions away from a predominantly northerly declination is consistent with post-middle W

ornquist sea, between Avalon and Baltica (Mac Niocaill and Smethurst, 1994). Upper Ordovician to Middle Devonian units in the northern Appalachians are generally brack- eted by Taconic and Acadian unconformities (Malo and Bourque, 1993). The Taconic orogenic pulse is associated with island arc accretion; the Silurian Salinic disturbance is associated with Avalonian col- lision and Iapetan closure; and the Acadian orogeny correlates with Devonian approach of Gondwana to Laurentia (van der Pluijm et al., 1993a; Van der Voo, 1993). The Silurian and Devonian rocks of the north- ern Appalachians form part of an overstep sequence deposited over the Central Mobile Belt. Silurian sed- imentary rocks form a southeast thickening wedge of shallow marine sedimentary rocks that grade from platformal carbonates in the northwest to central basinal shales and non-marine sandstones in the southeast (Keppie and Dostal, 1994). Silurian sed- iments were mainly derived from Laurentia to the northwest, whereas Lower Devonian flysch was derived from Avalon to the southeast. The Pis- cataquis and Tobique volcanic belts cross-cut the general structural trend of the northern Appalachi- ans (Fig. 1). Fivemile Brook results AMS results indicate a low degree of anisotropy, indicating minimal probability of remanence deflec- tion. The ratios of bulk susceptibilities at 77 K to those at room temperature (293 K) indicate involve- ment of a paramagnetic mineral phase that is proba- bly chlorite. Moreover, the magnetic fabric observed in a number of Fivemile Brook sites is roughly cleavage parallel. Based on high unblocking temperatures it is in- ferred that both the c- and b-components are carried by hematite. In view of the extremely high tem- peratures required to thermally reset hematite grains (Pullaiah et al., 1976), both the c- and b-components are presumably chemical remanent magnetizations (CRMs) resulting from hematite replacement of orig- inal magnetite. Subaerial weathering may account for initial oxidation of the magnetite in these vol- canics; a later CRM may be associated with fluid circulation (Dorobek, 1989). The approximately antipodal directions are in- terpreted as a record of geomagnetic field rever- sals. The c-component clearly passes the common kappa reversal test. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) mea- surements were made using a Kappabridge KLY-2 susceptibility bridge with each specimen being mea- sured in 15 orientations. Comparisons of the in- tensity of the susceptibility at room temperature with that at 77 K were made for four represen- tative samples to examine the source of suscep- tibility in Fivemile Brook specimens (Richter and van der Pluijm, 1993). Natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) directions and intensities were measured with a triple-axis 2G superconducting magnetometer. Alternating field demagnetization of a few specimens revealed a high coercivity and, therefore, did not suc- cessfully separate the components. The majority of the specimens were thermally demagnetized in an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer, using typically one specimen per sample, but occasionally two. Both demagnetization and measurement were done in the magnetically shielded room. After visual inspection of orthogonal vector endpoint diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967), principal component analysis was used to cal- culate component directions (Kirschvink, 1980) and the results are summarized in Tables 1-3. The inclination-only fold test peaks at 50% unfolding with a mean inclination of -35 ° (~ = 8.5 °, n = 148). Synfolding acquisition of magnetization is Wenlockian, based on a negative conglomerate test at the base of the section and a positive conglomerate test at the top of the section. ornquist sea, between Avalon and Baltica (Mac Niocaill and Smethurst, 1994). Upper Ordovician to Middle Devonian units in the northern Appalachians are generally brack- eted by Taconic and Acadian unconformities (Malo and Bourque, 1993). The Taconic orogenic pulse is associated with island arc accretion; the Silurian Salinic disturbance is associated with Avalonian col- lision and Iapetan closure; and the Acadian orogeny correlates with Devonian approach of Gondwana to Laurentia (van der Pluijm et al., 1993a; Van der Voo, 1993). The Silurian and Devonian rocks of the north- ern Appalachians form part of an overstep sequence deposited over the Central Mobile Belt. Silurian sed- imentary rocks form a southeast thickening wedge of shallow marine sedimentary rocks that grade from platformal carbonates in the northwest to central basinal shales and non-marine sandstones in the southeast (Keppie and Dostal, 1994). Silurian sed- iments were mainly derived from Laurentia to the northwest, whereas Lower Devonian flysch was derived from Avalon to the southeast. The Pis- cataquis and Tobique volcanic belts cross-cut the general structural trend of the northern Appalachi- ans (Fig. 1). The palaeolatitude of Hainan Island is 25.9ëN ( C3.4ë=/NUL3.2ë), implying that Hainan island was situated about 7ë north from the present position during the Cretaceous. The palaeopole of Hainan Island (latitude D 77.7ëN, longitudeD 162.1ëE, kD 65:6, and A 95 D 4:4ë) suggests 4:0 5:8ë counterclockwise rotation and 14 :1 5:5ë southward translation relative to the suspected coherent part of the south China block (SCB) since the Cretaceous. The rotation and translation of similar sense (18:8 7:4ë and 7:8 6:9ë, respectively) are detected in the existing palaeomagnetic result from the Xinlong Formation in Guangxi, which is situated approximately 400 km north-northwest from Hainan Island. The southward translation of both areas seems to have been due to the southeastward extrusion of dissected zones within the southwestern part of the SCB in a similar pattern to the Indochina block, which had resulted from the indentation of India into Asia. This SW part seems to have slightly rotated counterclockwise, because its extrusion was probably smaller in scale than the Indochina block and therefore it was dragged out by the Indochina block. Usually, after about 60% of remanent magnetization was removed at 250ëC, magnetization directions became unsta- ble probably due to weak magnetization or ther- mochemical alteration. In this case, samples were subjected to a hybrid demagnetization technique, in which thermal demagnetization up to 250ëC or 300ëC is followed by AF demagnetization up to about 100 mT. All the demagnetization results were plotted as orthogonal diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) and stereographic projections. The magnetic com- ponents were separated using principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980). 4.1. Magnetic component analysis Most samples of the lower Paleozoic display a simple demagnetization behavior during AF, thermal or hybrid demagnetization (Figs. 5 and 6). Gener- ally, after removing the present geomagnetic ®eld overprints or viscous remanent magnetizations at the beginning of demagnetization, a higher temperature or coercivity component is isolated from most of the samples. One group of directions (labeled component A) clusters mostly in the northwest with downward shallow to moderate inclination and its antipode af- ter tilt correction. This component is unblocked at B. The Clearwater anorthosite offers the pos- sibility of a pre-2.1 Ga age because it appears in- terlayered and folded with Archean gneisses of the Western Granulite Domain and may have been up- lifted before 2.1 Ga. If the Superior and Rae=Hearne provinces contain magmatic products related to the opening of the Manikewan ocean, then prior to 2.1 Ga they may have been joined. In this paper we test this idea through the use of paleomagnetism, anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and Ar±Ar geochronology, by searching for a possible pre-2.1 Ga uplift-related remanence that might be compared to well-dated magnetizations in the Su- perior Province such as those from the 2167 Ma Biscotasing and 2216 Ma Seneterre dyke swarms (Buchan et al., 1993). 2. Geology The Clearwater complex comprises a layered cumulate sequence dominated by anorthosite and anorthositic norite to gabbro (Scott, 1985; Hulbert, 1988). The rocks are often extremely fresh with primary calcic plagioclase, clinopyroxene, orthopy- roxene and olivine. The complex exhibits primary layering, which dips on average about 35ëSE and is normally expressed by

egmatite dykes and granitic sheets locally cut the anorthosite and may be related to this event (Crocker et al., 1993). 3. Methodology 3.1. Paleomagnetism About 120 samples, each oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses, were ®eld-drilled at 13 sites mainly in anorthosite, along a 7.5 km long traverse oriented normal to strike (Fig. 3). Since outcrops often form high knolls, care was taken to sample around their base to avoid ubiq- uitous lightning strikes at higher elevations which caused spalling of the weathered surface and differ- ences between magnetic and sun compass readings. The samples were subject to alternating ®eld (AF) and thermal demagnetization using Schonstedt de- magnetizer models GSD-1 and TSD-1, respectively. After removal of a low-temperature component of magnetisation, (L), interpreted to represent a viscous component of the earth's present ®eld, a high-temperature component of magnetisation, (H), was isolated at ®fteen sites in four ignimbrite ¯ows. H passes a palaeomagnetic fold test yielding a tilt-corrected mean remanence direction DD 132:6ë, ID 29:1ë, 95D 17:9ë which corresponds to a palaeopole at 36.4ëE, 9.9ëS. The pole is in reasonable agreement with established Early to middle Ordovician reference poles for Laurentia and indicates that no signi®cant rotation occurred between the E±W South Mayo Trough and the Laurentian margin after accretion, and therefore that the curvature of this segment of the orogen is likely to be primary. We report the results of a palaeomagnetic investigation of the Early to middle Ordovician Mweelrea Ignimbrites (Llanvirn), from an accreted Taconic arc (the South Mayo Trough) in that part of the western Irish Caledonides that has an E±W trend. After removal of a low-temperature component of magnetisation, (L), interpreted to represent a viscous component of the earth's present ®eld, a high-temperature component of magnetisation, (H), was isolated at ®fteen sites in four ignimbrite ¯ows. H passes a palaeomagnetic fold test yielding a tilt-corrected mean remanence direction DD 132:6ë, ID 29:1ë, 95D 17:9ë which corresponds to a palaeopole at 36.4ëE, 9.9ëS. The pole is in reasonable agreement with established Early to middle Ordovician reference poles for Laurentia and indicates that no signi®cant rotation occurred between the E±W South Mayo Trough and the Laurentian margin after accretion, and therefore that the curvature of this segment of the orogen is likely to be primary. This contrasts with other results from Silurian sequences to the south, which record signi®cant post-Silurian clockwise rotati

lway (Smethurst et al., 1994), but the full geographic extent of the rotated units could not be determined. Therefore the issue remains as to what proportion of the arcuate fea- tures are secondary, and what proportion are primary. To address this problem, we conducted a palaeo- magnetic investigation of the Mweelrea Ignimbrites (Llanvirn), in the South Mayo Trough (SMT) which lies to the north of our previous studies in the Sil- urian of north Galway. The palaeomagnetism of the Mweelrea Ignimbrites has been studied by Deutsch and Somayajulu (1969) and Morris (1973). Although both studies yielded qualitative evidence for a pri- mary magnetic remanence approximately concor- dant with that expected for Laurentia (Briden et al., 1989), the results are based on limited demagneti- sation procedures and have large error margins. The Deutsch and Somayajulu (1969) study, in particular, was also characterised by a rather limited geographi- cal coverage of sampling sites. Neither of the earlier palaeomagnetic studies addressed the possibility of within-terrane relative rotation. 34 C. Mac Niocaill et al. / Tectonophysics 299 (1998) 31±47 2. In this scheme the Early Ordovician comprises the Tremadoc and Arenig (495±480 and 480±470 Ma, respectively), the middle Ordovician consists of the Llanvirn series (470±458 Ma) and the Late Ordovi- cian comprises the Caradoc and Ashgill (458±449 and 449±443 Ma, respectively). The Silurian is sub- divided into four series: the Llandovery (443±428 Ma), the Wenlock (428±423 Ma), the Ludlow (423± 419 Ma) and the Pridoli (419±417 Ma). The Mweelrea Ignimbrites form part of the Mweelrea Formation, a 2-km (minimum)-thick se- quence of coarse-grained, trough cross-bedded sand- stones with local conglomerates and slates exposed in the SMT. Abdeldayem 1 Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Tanta Uni˝ersity, Tanta, Egypt Received 22 September 1998; accepted 25 September 1998 Abstract The palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic characteristics of some Cenozoic rocks from the Cairo±Fayum area have been .investigated. A total number of 259 oriented core samples were collected at 32 sites located in rocks of Eocene 13 sites , .  .Oligocene 11 sites and Pliocene 9 sites ages. Most of these rocks carry a weak but stable remanent magnetisation that is principally carried by hematite. Goethite and magnetite are also found in some samples as subordinate constituents. Careful thermal demagnetisation successfully enabled the isolation of the characteristic remanent magnetisation. Normal and reversed polarities that passed a reversal test have been recorded in the three age groups. This magnetisation is probably of primary origin and reflects the ages of the rocks. The resultant palaeomagnetic poles are considered reliable and represent a good contribution to the African palaeomagnetic database and should help in further refining of the Cenozoic APWP for Africa. q 1999 Elsevier Science

Abdeldayem 1 Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Tanta Uni˝ersity, Tanta, Egypt Received 22 September 1998; accepted 25 September 1998 Abstract The palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic characteristics of some Cenozoic rocks from the Cairo±Fayum area have been .investigated. A total number of 259 oriented core samples were collected at 32 sites located in rocks of Eocene 13 sites , .  .Oligocene 11 sites and Pliocene 9 sites ages. Most of these rocks carry a weak but stable remanent magnetisation that is principally carried by hematite. Goethite and magnetite are also found in some samples as subordinate constituents. Careful thermal demagnetisation successfully enabled the isolation of the characteristic remanent magnetisation. Normal and reversed polarities that passed a reversal test have been recorded in the three age groups. This magnetisation is probably of primary origin and reflects the ages of the rocks. Palaeomagnetic measurements In the present study new palaeomagnetic results from Tertiary volcanic occurrences of the Siebenge- birge and the Westerwald are presented. These vol- canic ®elds are located at the northeastern part of the Rhenish Massif (Fig. 12). The new palaeomagnetic results are compared with (1) the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of Tertiary central Europe and Ð giving even more evidence Ð (2) with palaeo- magnetic results of the neighbouring volcanic areas Hocheifel, V ogelsberg and RhoÈn, which were active at about the same time period. Older palaeomag- netic results from Siebengebirge and Westerwald derived from Nairn and Ku Èrsten (1959) and Nairn (1962) did not seem to be very reliable because of missing detailed demagnetization experiments and corresponding analyses of remanent magnetization. Here we present the results of our new palaeomag- netic investigations of 36 sites of the Westerwald and 19 sites of the Siebengebirge Tertiary volcanic ®elds (Rotsch, 1997; Fig. 1, Table 1). 2.1. Results for the 55 sites may be summarized as follows. The material can roughly be divided into two groups: LT1-3 (more than 60% of the sites) with low Curie temperatures below 300ëC, and HT1-5 with Curie temperatures between 300ëC and 650ëC (Fig. 2). Samples of the ®rst group are supposed to contain unexsolved tita- nium-rich titanomagnetite (TM40±TM75). Accordingly, samples were mainly taken from quarries with fresh rock material out- crops. To get an overview of the palaeodirections in both volcanic ®elds, it was tried to sample as many sites distributed all over the whole volcanic ®elds as possible. Furthermore, sampling was focused es- pecially on isotopically dated sites. This enabled us to compare the recorded palaeodirections from the Siebengebirge and the Westerwald with results from surrounding volcanic regions and with the APWP compilations for Tertiary central Europe. Isotopic dating (whole rock dating and 40Ar=39Ar mineral dating) of 21 sites in the Siebengebirge and 19 sites in the Westerwald by Lippolt and Todt (1978) and Todt and Lippolt (1980) shows, that the main pe- riod of Tertiary volcanic activity for both volcanic ®elds can be dated back to the time span of 22± 30 Ma. However, in some cases isotopic ages were found to be in contradiction to geological facts (e.g. Schreiber, 1996). The sinistral Tsushima±Goto tectonic line is the most probable tectonic boundary in the west of SW Japan (Ishikawa et al., 1989). A large clockwise block rotation by dextral move- ment of the Yangsan Fault on the Korean Peninsula occurred at 17.3 Ma, and is interpreted as revealing a parallel spreading event before a fan-shaped rota- tional event of the Japanese Islands (at around 15 Ma) during the opening of the East Sea. Much more paleomagnetic data (for example, for Cenozoic rocks in the Yeonil Basin) is needed to clarify rotational time, tectonic process and mecha- nism of the Pohang area. In this study, paleomag- netic results are presented for the Tertiary volcanic and sedimentary rocks from both the Yeonil and Yangnam Basins in the southern part of the Ko- rean Peninsula in order to obtain more informations about the time of the clockwise rotation event of the area. We also obtained new paleomagnetic data for the Eocene V olcanic Rocks in the Yeonil Basin offering more concrete tectonic scheme of the area. The analysis of the results combined with previous data suggests a probable model of opening of the East Sea, which is interpreted as correlating with northward migration of the Philippine Sea Plate. 2. A large clockwise block rotation by dextral move- ment of the Yangsan Fault on the Korean Peninsula occurred at 17.3 Ma, and is interpreted as revealing a parallel spreading event before a fan-shaped rota- tional event of the Japanese Islands (at around 15 Ma) during the opening of the East Sea. These are northward declinations in the Middle Miocene Yeonil Group and strong eastward declinations in the Early Miocene Yangbuk Group and in the Eocene V olcanic Rocks. However, the ®t was not typically good because of a weak anomaly am- plitude of 200±300 nT especially in the western part of the East Sea (Isezaki and Uyeda, 1973). Based on the magnetic anomaly lineations, Isezaki (1986) pro- posed that the opening started at 19 Ma and ceased at 15 Ma in the Japan Basin when the half spreading rate was assumed to be 3.4 cm =year. Kono (1986) found that a typical wavelength of 30 to 50 km in the eastern part of the East Sea represents a ¯uctuation of Miocene geomagnetic reversal polarity of 0.3± 0.5 Ma scale when the spreading rate was assumed as about 10 cm =year. He pointed out that the dif®- culty of identifying the magnetic pro®le in the East Sea because of the possibilities of spreading from multiple ridges or frequent ridge jumps, a distorted skewness by later thermal events or block motion in the crust, and a deep or thin magnetic source layer. He proposed a one-sided spreading model for the East Sea opening during Anomalies 5B (15 Ma) to 5AA (13 Ma) with a ridge jump at 5AC (14 Ma). 6. The sinistral Tsushima±Goto tectonic line is the most probable tectonic boundary in the west of SW Japan (Ishikawa et al., 1989). This idea is strongly sup- ported by the considerable counterclockwise block rotations around 15 Ma based on paleomagnetic data from the Tsushima and Goto Islands (Ishikawa and Tagami, 1991) and the existence of compressive de- formation and thrust belts, 100 km wide (Fig. 9c), about northwestern SW Japan. 10. Conclusions Dual polarity paleomagnetic data obtained from Tertiary rocks in the southeastern Korean Peninsula indicate a close relationship with the opening of the East Sea. A large clockwise block rotation by dextral move- ment of the Yangsan Fault on the Korean Peninsula occurred at 17.3 Ma, and is interpreted as revealing a parallel spreading event before a fan-shaped rota- tional event of the Japanese Islands (at around 15 Ma) during the opening of the East Sea. target_context.excerpt: act Two different distributions of declinations with dual polarities are found in the Tertiary rocks of the Yeonil Basin and Yangnam Basin along the Yangsan Fault in the southeastern part of the Korean Peninsula. These are northward declinations in the Middle Miocene Yeonil Group and strong eastward declinations in the Early Miocene Yangbuk Group and in the Eocene V olcanic Rocks. This is interpreted by invoking (1) the Yangsan Fault as a dextral wrench fault system by spreading in the Uleung Basin of the East Sea (Sea of Japan), and (2) a clockwise vertical rotation caused by the movement of the fault at around 17.3 Ma just prior to the sedimentation of the Yeonil Group. The Gingenbullen Dolerite (GB) (34.5°S, 150.3°E) and the Gibraltar Microsyenite (GS) (34.5°S, 150.4°E) were emplaced during the second of three major phases of igneous activity that aVected the southern Sydney Basin and are K/Ar dated at 172 and 178 Ma, respectively. The magnetic mineralogy of the two intrusions is diVerent: the GB is dominated by single-domain (SD)/pseudo-single-domain grains of magnetite, whereas the GS has both SD magnetite and haematite components, although the haematite component does not record a stable remanence. The GB records two opposed components of magnetization, above 100 °C, occupying distinct parts of the blocking temperature spectrum. The lower blocking temperature (LBT) component resides between 150 and 400 °C and is of normal polarity, having a mean direction of D/I=021°/−79° (a95=8°, k=63), with a corresponding VGP at Lat/Long = 54°S/137°E( dp=12, dm=13). This component is believed to be a TCRM or TVRM related to the initial opening of the Tasman Sea at ~90 Ma. T

The Gingenbullen Dolerite (GB) (34.5°S, 150.3°E) and the Gibraltar Microsyenite (GS) (34.5°S, 150.4°E) were emplaced during the second of three major phases of igneous activity that aVected the southern Sydney Basin and are K/Ar dated at 172 and 178 Ma, respectively. The magnetic mineralogy of the two intrusions is diVerent: the GB is dominated by single-domain (SD)/pseudo-single-domain grains of magnetite, whereas the GS has both SD magnetite and haematite components, although the haematite component does not record a stable remanence. The GB records two opposed components of magnetization, above 100 °C, occupying distinct parts of the blocking temperature spectrum. This component is believed to be a TCRM or TVRM related to the initial opening of the Tasman Sea at ~90 Ma. The Gingenbullen Dolerite (GB) (34.5°S, 150.3°E) and the Gibraltar Microsyenite (GS) (34.5°S, 150.4°E) were emplaced during the second of three major phases of igneous activity that aVected the southern Sydney Basin and are K/Ar dated at 172 and 178 Ma, respectively. The magnetic mineralogy of the two intrusions is diVerent: the GB is dominated by single-domain (SD)/pseudo-single-domain grains of magnetite, whereas the GS has both SD magnetite and haematite components, although the haematite component does not record a stable remanence. This component is believed to be a TCRM or TVRM related to the initial opening of the Tasman Sea at ~90 Ma. T

They date from around 197 Ma and the flows are mainly tholeiitic basalts with a low TiO 2 and incompatible element content. The magnetic carriers in rocks from these two formations were highly oxidized titanomagnetites, maghemites and, probably, titanomaghemites. Paleomagnetic analysis has shown that the magneti- zations are all normal in polarity and virtual geomagnetic poles obtained for both formations are indistinguishable at the 95% confidence level. The calculated mean for these poles is 250.3°E, 65.5°S (N = 15; A95 = 3.6°; Ksc = 1578). This pole is compatible with Jurassic poles which have been determined for South America or transposed from Africa. 1. The type b, c, and d curves are character- istic 9f titanomagnetites that have undergone low temperature oxidation ([33-35] and references therein). Titanomagnetites that have undergone a low temperature oxidation can be transformed into titanomaghemites, when thermomagnetic curves will be irreversible. Although curves of type b, c and d are typical of titanomaghemites they could also represent titanomagnetites with high Ti content. Samples corresponding to type b curves (CT 382-418°C; Fig. 6B) have, in general, not yielded favorable paleomagnetic results. A probable explanation is that the magnetic carriers (probably titanomaghemites) had low CTs and blocking temperatures (Fig. 6B, b) and were not able to preserve the primary remanent magneti- zation which, as indicated by data, corresponds to samples of type a, c and d curves. Thermomag- netic curves of type c and d, show a low CT (365-393°C) magnetic phase but it is not unique. In both cases the palaeomagnetic rotation is consistent with the regional superstructure of the Hindukush–Pamir–Karakoram syntaxial bend. The di Verence in rotation between these two groups is probably due to local tectonic movement caused by the net rotation of thrust sheets along the Northern Suture Zone. The palaeolatitudes calculated for Purit and Reshun +Drosh formations are 2.2 ° S and 1.1 ° N, respectively. This indicates that about 4000 km of convergence has taken place since the mid-Cretaceous, of which about 90 per cent post-dates the India–Asia collision. The Late Cretaceous inclination values across the Northern Suture Zone are almost identical, which indicates that suturing had been completed at the time of ChRM acquisition.
